prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, enabling measurement of time and frequency at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: In my opening ballot I placed the Higgs experiments first and the optical lattice clock second. Having read all eight ballots I now put the clock first. It meets the criteria I apply most strictly: an original idea (Katori's magic-wavelength trapping, which removes the lattice light shift while atoms are held in the Lamb-Dicke regime), an experimental demonstration, independent reproduction in many laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE and others) and a measurable consequence, namely fractional uncertainties near 10^-18, relativistic redshift resolved over millimetres, tests of the constancy of constants, and the coming redefinition of the second. It is a new tool that opens a door to phenomena nobody could measure before. It is also the only shortlisted candidate that all eight members ranked, and six of the eight placed it in their top three. Its attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: a two-person split between the originator of the concept and first realisation (Katori) and the person who pushed it to record accuracy and many-body regimes (Ye).
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that this is an instrument and precision advance built on two recently recognised steps, the frequency comb (2005) and single-ion control and clocks (2012), so a sceptical member can call it a refinement and not a discovery. Because I insist that the prize is not for the second discoverer who did it better, I must test that charge honestly. The clock is a distinct invention, because it needs a different physical idea (the magic wavelength) and does not follow from the comb or from ion traps. Even so, the redefinition of the second has not happened yet, and a member who wants that milestone first has a fair argument for waiting. A second weakness is that I may be undervaluing the Higgs case, which I still regard as the purest 'original experiment' on the list. It is held back only by the difficulty of naming three people from two collaborations of thousands.

responses.point: The optical lattice clock is the cleanest case on the list of a new method that changed what can be measured. Katori and Ye form the natural pair, but the committee may debate who is the primary originator and whether the wider Sr/Yb/Hg community deserves credit.
responses.response: I agree with the merit argument and with the two-person split. On the originator question the record favours Katori on priority: the magic-wavelength proposal and the first strontium lattice clock come from his group. Ye's decisive contribution is a different kind, namely taking the clock to systematic uncertainty and stability at the 10^-18 level and showing many-body effects. The prize is for the invention and development, so crediting the originator and the person who made it a precision instrument is not a lifetime-achievement award. I would still ask that the committee check the chronology against the 2003 to 2005 papers, because Kroll and others, including me, are working partly from memory.

responses.point: The clock is clear and well replicated, but the committee must be convinced it is distinct enough from the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 ion-clock prize, and the pending redefinition of the second might make recognition better timed later.
responses.response: I take the overlap objection seriously, since I apply the original-experiment test strictly. My answer is that the 2005 prize rewarded the comb as a frequency ruler, and the 2012 prize rewarded control of single quantum systems. Neither covers a many-atom neutral-atom clock operated at a magic wavelength, so the credit does not duplicate. On timing I disagree with waiting. The performance is already independently verified in many laboratories, and the Nobel Prize should not depend on a metrological body's schedule. I also note that you rank circuit QED first, and I do not dismiss it. My hesitation is that the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits sits very close, and I would want the committee to be sure it is not recognising the same community again so soon.

responses.point: Topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect are original, conceptually clean and have reshaped condensed-matter physics, with Kane and Mele on theory and Molenkamp on the HgTe experiment, giving a strong theory-plus-experiment prize.
responses.response: I ranked this third and share your view of its scientific importance and maturity. My reservation is about whether the three names capture the original work. The HgTe observation by Molenkamp's group followed the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, and the 3D topological insulators involve Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore and Balents, so omitting them could misstate who did the original work. Kane and Mele also cannot carry the whole 3D story. Mehlig and Johansson raise the same attribution problem, and the 2016 topology prize adds another question. If the committee can show a defensible three-person set, I would support it as the alternative, but at present the attribution is harder to defend than for the clock.

responses.point: The Higgs boson was found by two independent experiments and is a landmark that completed the Standard Model, but only three of four names can be chosen, with Jenni and Virdee representing the two experiments' conception, and the committee has been reluctant to credit experiment leaders.
responses.response: We agree on the importance, and this is why the Higgs experiments are my first alternative. Our slates differ at one position: you choose Virdee on the CMS side, and I chose Della Negra, both founders of CMS. I do not think the scientific record settles that choice, and I explain below why I am not preferring this configuration. The committee would be crediting a leadership role in a collaboration of thousands, and I cannot be 'absolutely sure' that the named people did the original work, as opposed to leading those who did. That is an attribution reservation, not a doubt about the discovery. If colleagues can agree on a principled rule, such as the proposers and spokespersons at the time of discovery, I would move it back to first place.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the clock as distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and whether the ion-versus-lattice credit division is acceptable.

The exact chronology and relative priority of Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, the first strontium lattice clock demonstrations, and contributions of other groups (Lemonde, Takamoto, Hollberg and others), which I cannot verify at this stage.
Whether a principled rule for naming three people from the ATLAS and CMS collaborations exists; if so, B054 should be reconsidered.
statement.conflict_note: No personal conflict is apparent from my profile for B048. I flag two institutional links for the chair: since 2025 I have been a Fellow of the University of Tokyo and have long-running exchanges with Tokyo-area microscopy communities, while Katori is a Tokyo-based researcher, though I have no known collaboration with him or Ye. Separately, my Chalmers colleague Göran Johansson's first choice (B001) is a different candidate. I regard these as grounds for disclosure only, not recusal, and I will follow the chair's view.
